To the PRINTER of The ST. JAMES's
CHRONICLE.

Mr. Baldwin,
BEING a great Lover and Admirer of the
Polite Arts, I never fail to attend the
annual Exhinitions of Pictures, &c. in this
Town; and though I do not profess myself
a Connoisseur, yet I commonly find that they
who judge naturally are as often in the right
as those who affect to pronounce scientifically.
Poets and Painters write and paint to all the
World, and they are never much pleased with
the Success of their Works, when they pro-
cure no other Commmendations than those of
their Brother-Artists. The Arts themselves,
though taught by Rules, are sounded in Na-
ture, and there are few Persons who cannot
in some Degree distinguish the comparative
Excellence of the Professors. Who that has
Eyes, but immediately sees and confesses the
Excellence of the elegant Productions of
the Hand of Reynolds? Does the Merit of
Cotes escape the most careless and unistruct-
ed Observerd? And to not all acknowledge the
bold and faithful Portraits of Gainsborough?
Emboldened by these Considerations, I
shall venture to send you a few Observations
which occured to me on seeing some of the
Pictures in the Collection now exhibiting at
Spring Gardens; and my Remarks may per-
haps at least have one good Effect; I shall
start Game for your Correspondents, which
perhaps they may be better qualified to run
down; and if I am wrong, the Publick may
be instructed and entertained by him that
shall take the Pains to correct me.
Mr. HAMILTON, at ROME.
No. 46. Achilles lamenting the Death of Pa-
troclus. -Great Encouragement should be given
to those Painters, who cultivate the nobler
Provinces of the Art, and endeavour to touch
the Passions by historical or poetical Pieces,
rather than to sacrifice to the Vanity of Man-
kind by Portrait-Painting. The Piece before
us is not witout Merit, but the Legs of Pa-
troclus do not appear like those of a dead
Man. Perhaps it would be impossible for
those of a dead Person to be in that Position,
in which the Picture exhibits those of Pa-
troclus.
Mr. HAYMAN, in St. Martin's Lane.
48. Sigismunda. -A very woeful Picture!
very sad indeed!
49. -Falstaff recruiting. -Falstaff the worst
Figure in the Piece. Shallow the best.- This
is a favourite Subject of Mr. H's.
Hayman, dull Mannerist!
52. Porsrats es a Ernilinan. An excellent
CHURCHILL.
52. Portraits of a Gentleman. -An excellent
Portrait.
53. Ditto.-Ditto.
54. Ditto of a Lady.-This is the Portrait
of a Lady, whose Charms are well known to the
Town.-The Painter has ingeniously attempted
to acquaint us with the Name by a Rebus
upon Canvas. By her Side, a Kitten [KITTY]
is attempting to get into a Bason of Gold Fish
[KITTY FISH-]-what Pity it is, he did not

52. Whole Lenght of a Lady.-A Piece of
great Merit. This is not the [?] Pro-
duction which we have seen from the Hand of
Mr. James.
Mr. KITTLE, Great Queen-Street, Lin-
coln's-Inn-Fields.
64. Portrait of a Lady, whole Length - This
is intended to represent Mrs Yates in the
Character of Mandane, in the Orphan of
China; but Mr. Kettle has by no Means
done Justice to the Beauty of Mrs. Yates.-
This Kettle is just the Opposite of the Kettle of
Medea which renewed Youth; for the Copy
appear twenty Years older than the Ori-
ginal.
Mr. HENRY LEAKE, Leicester-Fields.
73. Mr. Powell, in the Character of Posthu-
mus. - A good Likeness of Mr. Powell. I
think, however, the Character of Posthumus
might have afforded some more interesting
Crisis, some picturesque Moment of Passion,
in the 3^d or last Act of the Play of Cymbe-
line.
Mr. PENNY, Mortimer-Street.
96. An Officer relieving a sick Soldier.-The
sick Soldier and his Family are happily ima-
gined, and well executed. The Officer,
which seems intended for the Marquis of
Granby, not so well.
97. The Return from a Fair. -A natural
Scene, somewhat in the Manner of Hogarth.
Mr. WEST, Castle-Street.
There is great Delicacy both in the Idea
and Execution of this Painter's Pieces. But
there is a Glow in his Colouring which gives
a Kind of unnatural Varnish to his Pictures.
There seems also to be a Sameness in his Fi-
gures, which, if not carefully avoided, will
obtain the Artist the Name of a Mannerist.
Perhaps also they are too delicate. It is dan-
gerous to attempt to exhibit Forms more beauti-
ful than those of Nature.
Mr. ZAFFANIS, Lincoln's-Inn Fields
167. Mr. Garrick's, drunken Scene in the
Provoked Wife.
168. A Family Piece.-Both these Pieces
have great Merit. In the first we have not
only a good Likeness of Mr. Garrick, but al-
so of Messrs. Vaughan, Clough, Parsons,
Philips, &c. whom it is impossible not to
know at first Sight. Mr. Zaffanis is peculi-
arly happy at taking Likeness. Some may
call this a mere Sign-Post Excellence, but
surely a Portrait is not worth a Farthing with-
out it.
I am, S IR,
Your constant Reader.
No Connoisseur.
